title: Bara Masa, Tera Parba: osha, story and food
scope: Eighteen selected profiles: seven narrative checkpoints and eleven research notes. Includes Nuakhai as a parba; no exhaustive inventory or completed origin histories claimed.

pages.name: Khudurukuni Osha
pages.lead: A small offering of rice carries a story of hunger, a sister’s hope and brothers away at sea.

sections.title: The story remembered
sections.text: In Deeti Ray’s account, Tapoi is the only sister of seven merchant brothers. During their absence, most of her sisters-in-law mistreat her. She encounters girls worshipping Mangala and offers the little khuda she has, asking for help. Her brothers return and discover her suffering. This is a ritual narrative, not a verified biography.
sections.locator: 2020 article, Tapoi narrative following the evening ritual

sections.title: Girls as keepers of the observance
sections.text: Ray describes Bhadraba Sundays in coastal Odisha: gathering flowers, a sand image called balunka, rice-paste decoration and evening recitation. Her photographs identify Pattamundai in Kendrapara as one setting. Girls organise and perform the worship. The account documents a particular cultural tradition; it does not establish identical practice in every district.
sections.locator: 2020 article, ritual sequence; Balunka caption

sections.title: Food makes the story tangible
sections.text: Patra’s 2019 essay identifies khuda as rice particles offered to Mangala. He connects the observance with a text attributed to Gopinath Das and with coastal maritime memory. The food association is stronger than any claim that a specific voyage occurred. Ray’s English food glosses sometimes use bran or husk; these are not interchangeable food-processing terms. We retain khuda and leave its preparation-specific identification for an Odia text and cook’s account.
sections.locator: Patra printed p.48; Ray food-offerings paragraph

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: An editorial reading of this story asks who receives care when a household’s earners are absent. The offering matters because of the giver’s circumstances. A food article can therefore follow rice through work, unequal access and devotion, rather than treating it only as a recipe. This interpretation should be tested against the words of present-day observers.

sections.title: History still to establish
sections.text: A twentieth- or twenty-first-century description is evidence that a tradition was recorded then, not its starting date. Manuscript and printed witnesses of the Tapoi text need to be compared before assigning a composition date. The 2022 journal paper has been located, but its original file was not recovered in this pass. Ray’s two publications would remain one author’s research lineage.
sections.locator: Publication and attribution boundaries

questions: How is khuda named and prepared in this locality?
Which Tapoi book or oral version is recited, and who taught it?
How have the worship group and food sharing changed?

pages.name: Manabasa Gurubara
pages.lead: A measure of grain becomes a way to think about sustenance, dignity and who may share a meal.

sections.title: Lakshmi and the rejected devotee
sections.text: Balabhadra Ghadai retells the Lakshmi Purana associated with Balaram Das: Lakshmi honours Sriya, a devotee identified in the narrative as Chandala. Balabhadra objects to the visit, and Jagannath excludes Lakshmi. The conflict centres on caste and the goddess’s freedom to recognise devotion. This is the text’s story, not evidence that discrimination subsequently disappeared.
sections.locator: Cult of Goddess Mahalakshmi, printed p.102

sections.title: Hunger changes the argument
sections.text: The Mohantys’ 2021 essay describes the brothers’ hardship after Lakshmi leaves and reads the work as a challenge to caste barriers. Food becomes central to the dispute over authority. Our interpretation is that a household’s feeding labour is made visible through its withdrawal: those who dismiss its source discover their dependence on it.
sections.locator: Printed p.23, Lakshmi Purana discussion

sections.title: The meal and the recognition
sections.text: In Ghadai’s retelling, the hungry brothers reach Lakshmi’s new household. Told that its mistress is Chandala, they first attempt to cook for themselves and fail. They finally accept her cooked food, recognise its familiar preparation and reunite with her. The reversal makes exclusion answerable to the experience of hunger. Ghadai himself says the story’s time of formation is not definitely known.
sections.locator: Printed pp.103–104

sections.title: The household observance
sections.text: The same essay places the worship on Margasira Thursdays and identifies the mana or grain measure among its objects. Dash records khiri, khechudi, kakara and chakuli as associated foods. These are attributed examples, not a compulsory menu for every Thursday or home.
sections.locator: Mohanty p.23; Dash p.17

sections.title: A history of text, voice and work
sections.text: The next historical step is to identify dated editions and manuscripts of Lakshmi Purana and compare how they are read aloud. The author attribution alone does not date today’s menu or decorations. The collection should credit the reader, cook and person who draws the household designs, including work that a dish photograph would leave invisible.

sections.title: A visitor’s starting point
sections.text: Learn the meaning of the grain measure and ask a willing cook about one preparation. A shop selling chakuli does not provide access to a household’s Manabasa worship. A future tasting record needs its own date, provider and consent.

questions: Which edition or inherited oral passage is used?
Which offerings differ across the Thursdays?
What does the family say about Sriya and shared food?

pages.name: Sudasa Brata
pages.lead: A knotted thread and an offering of manda connect a recurring vow with Lakshmi.

sections.title: The vow and its objects
sections.text: The Mohantys describe a thread with ten knots, each associated with a name of Lakshmi. Mahanti gives the calendrical condition as a Thursday coinciding with the bright fortnight’s tenth lunar day; it can recur within a year. Dash’s Kartika-only description is therefore retained as a conflict, not used as the general rule.
sections.locator: Mohanty p.25; Mahanti p.43; Dash p.15

sections.title: Manda in the offering
sections.text: Dash names manda for Sudasa. The existing food record describes a steamed version, but that does not establish the recipe of every ritual offering. The useful questions concern dough, filling, cooking method, number and distribution. A dish name can remain stable while its preparation varies.
sections.locator: Printed pp.17–18

sections.title: Two stories around the vow
sections.text: In the scanned verse booklet, a kite takes a Brahmin woman’s ritual thread and the king gives her the queen’s brata; Nala and Damayanti later endure hardship before renewal and restoration. In the typed prose, a cat steals a merchant wife’s manda and King Sudarshana obtains a replacement from Queen Sudasha’s offering. The merchant’s wife later helps the queen renew the vow. The thread and the cake carry different narrative roles. Neither story establishes a historical event.
sections.locator: Verse printed pp.1–12; prose PDF pp.1–4

sections.title: What history can and cannot say
sections.text: The sources connect the brata to Lakshmi devotion, but no earliest Odisha performance is established here. Mahanti’s claim of revival by Balarama Das still needs a dated textual witness. The two recovered copies tell different stories, so neither is treated as a single authoritative original.
sections.locator: Printed p.43

sections.title: Reading its significance
sections.text: A useful editorial lens is the relationship between an enduring object and repeated action: a thread can remind its wearer of a vow between observances. This is a question to explore with practitioners, not an assertion that everyone gives the thread the same meaning.

sections.title: A printed offering passage
sections.text: An undated verse booklet naming Damayanti in its title describes ten manda with chhena and coconut filling. Damayanti is a character in its story, not an established author credit. The passage supplies a textual food reference while leaving the cooking method unresolved; it does not prove the observance’s starting date or a recipe followed by every household.
sections.locator: Printed pp.2–3, especially verse17 on p.2; PDF p.3

sections.title: Manuscripts to compare
sections.text: The National Mission for Manuscripts lists five Sudasa Brata Katha accessions: ORPR-64, ORPR-210, ORPR-220, ORPR-221 and ORPR-226. Their texts and copying dates remain unexamined; separate catalogue entries do not yet establish separate narrative variants.
sections.locator: PDF pp.20–21

questions: Which dated colophons establish the transmission of each story?
How do the two stories circulate in different localities?
Is manda steamed or fried in each documented household version, and what dough is used?

pages.name: Dutiya Osha
pages.lead: The path from offered produce to a shared ghanta is the beginning of this food story.

sections.title: A documented sequence
sections.text: Dash’s 2006 essay records fruits and vegetables offered during Dutiya Osha and cooked into ghanta the following day. He also mentions sand figures of a fox and a bird. The source groups several names together; we have not treated that as proof that every regional Jitiya or Puajiuntia tradition is identical.
sections.locator: Printed pp.15,17

sections.title: Food after the offering
sections.text: The important research unit is the sequence: gathering, offering, cooking and sharing. A recipe alone would miss the change in the produce’s ritual role. The next account should identify a particular household’s ghanta, its ingredients and recipients; it should also record omissions and substitutions. This is an editorial approach, not a measured claim about waste reduction or nutrition.

sections.title: The missing narrative
sections.text: The fox-and-bird figures point to a story that needs an identified local katha. This page deliberately does not import a neighbouring region’s narrative to fill the gap. No foundation date or earliest local manuscript has yet been established.

sections.title: For the seasonal guide
sections.text: Ghanta can be explored as a dish beyond this observance. A visitor listing must say whether a provider offers an everyday version or an observance-associated preparation, and on which confirmed dates.

sections.title: A coastal food account
sections.text: Mahanti describes a coastal observance on Ashwina’s dark eighth lunar day. His account offers twenty-one varieties of seasonal vegetables beneath an aparamanga leaf, then cooks them into ghanta tarkari for exchange. The number and leaf belong to this account; they are not a universal menu. The plant’s botanical identity remains unverified here.
sections.locator: Printed p.58, PDF p.74

sections.title: Manuscripts to compare
sections.text: Catalogue leads include Duti Bahana Osha at ORPR-106, Dwitia Osha at OL-2452, Ditiya Osha at OL/2673 and Dwitiya Osa at OL/2674. Similar titles are a reason to compare the texts, not evidence that they have identical stories or match every regional Puajiuntia tradition.
sections.locator: NMM PDF pp.21,45; museum OL/2673 and OL/2674

questions: What are the local name and bird identification in the katha?
Which produce is offered, and which is cooked the following day?
Who receives a share, and how is the dish named?

pages.name: Budhei Osha
pages.lead: Kitchen grinding stones open a line of inquiry into household worship and hopes for children.

sections.title: The record we have
sections.text: Dash places Budhei on Bhadraba Wednesdays and describes worship involving a grinding stone. Mahanti records fruit and pitha offerings, with a coconut kept from the first Wednesday to the last. Their deity identifications differ. We preserve those accounts rather than selecting one identity as definitive.
sections.locator: Dash p.15; Mahanti pp.56–57

sections.title: Everyday objects, sacred roles
sections.text: The grinding stone makes this a promising study of the relationship between food labour and household ritual. That is our research lens; the object alone cannot prove the observance began in a particular occupation, century or religious school. Its handling, decoration and return to everyday use need an attributed local account.

sections.title: Story and food gaps
sections.text: A full narrative needs a named Budhei or Budhibaman text and a comparison of its episodes. Neither a universal pitha menu nor a uniform fasting practice is established here. We should ask who selects the foods and how the final Wednesday differs, while leaving fertility and protection claims explicitly within belief.

sections.title: Manuscripts to compare
sections.text: Institutional catalogues identify Budhei texts at OL-2022, OL-2443 and OL/2636. The museum describes OL/2636 as palm leaf. These references make a comparison possible, but no copying date, earliest composition or food passage can yet be assigned from their catalogue entries.
sections.locator: NMM PDF pp.13,45; museum OL/2636

questions: Are Budhei, Sudhei and Budhibaman distinguished locally?
Which stories are read on successive Wednesdays?
What foods belong to the final observance?

pages.name: Alana Osha
pages.lead: A food restriction can be as culturally meaningful as a festive dish.

sections.title: Agreement and disagreement
sections.text: Dash describes Alana as an Ashwina observance without salt and associates it with Lakshmi. Mahanti also describes unsalted offerings but names Surya. This is an unresolved source difference; neither a single deity nor a uniform household practice is asserted.
sections.locator: Dash pp.15,17; Mahanti p.58

sections.title: Narrating restraint
sections.text: The next page should ask what observers mean by the restriction, what they actually prepare and when they resume ordinary food. It would be misleading to attach a generic sweet to Alana simply to fill a menu. A cultural description of abstention is not dietary advice or evidence of a health benefit.

sections.title: History to recover
sections.text: No securely dated origin or inspected local ritual narrative has been established. The conflict may involve regional variation, terminology or an error; that question needs evidence, not a harmonised story invented by the editor.

questions: Which deity and katha does the household recognise?
Does the restriction apply to offerings, the observer’s meals or both?

pages.name: Kanji Anla Osha
pages.lead: Rice-water preparations and a ritual offering invite a closer look at a less-documented part of the food year.

sections.title: What the sources describe
sections.text: Dash associates Kanji Anla with Sathi and lists kanji, radish and other materials. Mahanti describes kanji from fermented rice gruel and dried-fish offerings in an evening observance. The accounts should be compared locally; the study does not turn their lists into one standard recipe.
sections.locator: Dash pp.15,18 note 2; Mahanti p.60

sections.title: A food-science question
sections.text: There is a worthwhile distinction between recording a fermentation practice and measuring it. A future preparation record should identify ingredients, water, vessel, temperature, time and subsequent cooking. These variables are research questions; we have not tested this preparation, identified its organisms or demonstrated a probiotic benefit.

sections.title: The narrative remains open
sections.text: A local katha, historical editions and the relationship to Sathi or Sasthi need further study. The use of dried fish also means that a blanket claim that all osha offerings are vegetarian would erase relevant evidence. This page retains the difference without claiming every household follows it.
sections.locator: Printed p.60

food_names: dried fish in an attributed account
questions: Which kanji preparation and local name are used?
How do observers explain the offered materials?
How does the practice relate to Prathamastami in this locality?

pages.name: Bada Osha
pages.lead: A Shiva offering called gaja needs its own identity, separate from sweets sold under similar names.

sections.title: Food with a ritual form
sections.text: The Jagatsinghpur district gazetteer describes a steamed gaja offering shaped as a linga and snake, followed by the breaking of a fast. This is a district account, not a verified menu at every Shiva temple. The preparation must not be silently equated with the fried chhena gaja in an existing food catalogue.
sections.locator: Printed p.52, Bada Osha

sections.title: Why location matters
sections.text: Mahanti associates Bada Osha particularly with Dhabaleswar and gives Kartika’s bright thirteenth or fourteenth day. The Jagatsinghpur gazetteer mentions Kartika Purnima. We keep those calendar statements separate pending a temple-specific annual schedule and clarification of observance versus culmination.
sections.locator: Mahanti pp.58–59; gazetteer p.52

sections.title: History and significance
sections.text: The evidence supports a connection among fasting, offering and Shiva worship. An origin story needs a traceable text or temple account before being narrated as the local explanation. Even then, the legend and the dated history of the shrine will remain separate.

sections.title: A visitor’s next step
sections.text: A future guide can explain what the offering means, but temple access, crowd arrangements and distribution need current checks. No ticket, serving time or availability is established by this historical description.

questions: What does the Dhabaleswar authority call the offering and its preparation?
Which date marks the fast and which marks its breaking?

pages.name: Samba Dashami
pages.lead: An offering made in a child’s name makes a family’s hopes visible through food.

sections.title: The legend and the observance
sections.text: Dina Krishna Joshi’s 2013 essay recounts the belief that Samba, Krishna’s son, recovered from illness through devotion to Surya. It places the observance on Pausa’s bright tenth lunar day. The healing belongs to sacred narrative; it is neither clinical evidence nor a dated account of the festival’s beginnings.
sections.locator: Printed p.55

sections.title: A family written in food
sections.text: Joshi describes offerings associated with individual family members and foods including khichdi, ghadghadia tarkari, pitha and khiri. His account moves through morning, midday and evening acts of worship and subsequent sharing. This gives us a sequence to investigate, not a universal menu or timetable.
sections.locator: Printed p.55, Tradition

sections.title: Sun worship in the landscape
sections.text: A multidisciplinary 2015 study of Konark records Samba Dashami among traditions associated with Chandrabhaga. That association is distinct from the study’s investigation of a lost river. A ritual’s relationship to a place does not date the ritual or establish the location of every episode in its legend.
sections.locator: Printed p.94, Rituals and Festivals associated with the river

sections.title: What gives the food its meaning
sections.text: Our interpretive question is how an offering in someone’s name becomes a household memory. Which item belongs to which child? Does it remain the same after that person leaves home? Those questions could connect the historical reading with living family accounts, without claiming interviews have already taken place.

questions: When and why was a particular offering chosen?
Which foods and worship times differ locally?
Which Samba katha is recited?

pages.name: Prathamastami
pages.lead: Enduri’s leaf wrapping connects a food technique with an occasion centred on the eldest child.

sections.title: Family and food
sections.text: Mahanti describes honouring the eldest child, including new clothes and an offering of enduri. Odisha Tourism independently associates enduri with Prathamastami and describes turmeric-leaf wrapping with a coconut-jaggery filling. These support a cultural food connection, not a claim that enduri is unavailable at other times.
sections.locator: Mahanti p.59; Tourism Enduri Pitha section

sections.title: What the leaf contributes
sections.text: The existing enduri page is the preparation reference. The observance page asks a different question: how does making, offering and sharing that food express a family relationship? We should record the leaf, batter, filling, steamer and cook alongside the person being honoured, rather than allow the recipe to replace the occasion.

sections.title: The calendar and history
sections.text: Margasira is supported in the household account, but earlier indexed temple descriptions differed on the fortnight. The website therefore does not generate a current date. A dated panji and a locality-specific check are needed. The earliest evidence of the household practice is also still to be established.
sections.locator: Printed p.59; prior calendar-conflict register

questions: What role do maternal relatives play in this family’s celebration?
Which enduri version is used and who makes it?
What dated calendar governs the local observance?

pages.name: Sabitri Brata
pages.lead: Savitri’s conversation with Yama gives this observance a literary history that can be read directly.

sections.title: A woman follows and argues
sections.text: In the Mahabharata passage preserved in K. M. Ganguli’s translation, Satyavan collapses while collecting wood. When Yama takes his life, Savitri follows. She speaks about duty, friendship and compassion; Yama repeatedly grants boons while withholding Satyavan’s life. Her request for children through Satyavan exposes the contradiction. He is restored. The episode gives Savitri a sustained speaking and reasoning role, not merely a moment of passive waiting.
sections.locator: Vana Parva, section displayed as CCLXLV, printed pp.576–581

sections.title: Textual history is not a local origin date
sections.text: An epic passage is direct evidence for the story. It does not tell us when a particular Odisha household began its annual brata or when its food customs took shape. That requires Odia katha editions, local histories and carefully attributed practice accounts. The pan-Indian story and the regional observance are connected research subjects, not interchangeable records.
sections.locator: Scope of the inspected epic passage

sections.title: Seasonal offerings
sections.text: Mahanti records a Jyestha new-moon observance with fruit offerings. Exact fruit selections need a local account; no fixed shopping list is prescribed here. Food can be documented through its role as an offering and its sharing after the observance, with changes in seasonal availability left visible.
sections.locator: Printed p.45

sections.title: Significance to explore
sections.text: The literary conversation permits questions about resolve, love and moral reasoning. Present-day observers may emphasise different aspects. A responsible narrative should let those explanations coexist and avoid turning a description of married women’s practice into a duty imposed on readers.

questions: Which Odia Savitri katha is read?
Which fruits are chosen locally, and how are they shared?
What aspects of Savitri’s words matter most to the observer?

pages.name: Janhi Osha
pages.lead: A vegetable plant enters the ritual year through its flowers, not just through the kitchen.

sections.title: The surviving outline
sections.text: Dash associates Janhi with Tulsi worship and its culmination at Kumar Purnima. Mahanti describes girls arranging ridge-gourd flowers to reflect the moon’s changing appearance. He explicitly leaves its origin unknown. The descriptions provide a starting point for documentation, not a dated beginning or proof of a statewide pattern.
sections.locator: Dash p.15; Mahanti p.56

sections.title: Flowers, a song and an evening game
sections.text: In a 2015 account framed around Ganjam, Prafulla Chandra Mohanty connects the end of month-long Janhi worship with Kumar Purnima. He records a short song addressing the Janhi flower and describes a street game using cowries, seeds called Poi-chardia and lia/khai. The grain is a game material in that passage; the author does not identify it there as Janhi’s offering.
sections.locator: Printed p.45, right column; PDF p.54

sections.title: The offering belongs to a particular scene
sections.text: Mohanty describes kakara pitha offered to the moon near the Tulsi platform, then shared with friends addressed as Chanda. This is his Kumar Purnima account, not evidence that kakara is the daily offering throughout Janhi Osha.
sections.locator: Printed p.45 left column and p.46 left column; PDF pp.54–55

sections.title: A food-culture question without an invented menu
sections.text: Janhi is a food plant, but that does not establish ridge-gourd curry as the observance’s special dish. Its flowers have a ritual role in the inspected account. The study should document that role first and ask separately about offerings and meals. Keeping these distinctions protects a small tradition from being rewritten as a generic food festival.

sections.title: How to read the significance
sections.text: Read together, the flower arrangement, sung address, play and sharing suggest several ways a seasonal observance can organise social life. That is an editorial interpretation of the accounts. It does not establish how every family understands the practice, whether the same game survives today, or what visitors can attend. The plant’s ritual use and a cooked offering should be documented as different relationships.

sections.title: What to recover next
sections.text: The 2015 article preserves a song fragment, not a complete Janhi katha or a dated origin account. A search-index lead for Janhi Osha Katha in an April 1938 Gazette book list awaits inspection of the original; the failed fetch does not verify the entry or date the practice. Full songs, printed texts, locality-specific meanings and current participation arrangements remain open.

questions: Can the Gazette book-registration entry be inspected and the listed Janhi booklet located?
How does the complete song or katha explain the floral designs in a named locality?
Which foods belong specifically to Janhi, and which to its Kumar Purnima culmination?
Do local practitioners still recognise the game and Chanda friendship custom described in 2015?

pages.name: Chaitra Mangala Osha
pages.lead: A Tuesday gathering, a seasonal drink and a story about a woman confronting royal power offer three ways into Mangala’s spring observance.

sections.title: The seasonal gathering
sections.text: Dash places Mangala worship on Tuesdays in Chaitra. Mahanti describes mostly married women gathering under a tree, shaping an image on sand or earth and decorating it with cloth and flowers. At midday they offer seasonal fruits and pana, accompanied by conches, bells and women’s ululation. This is an attributed description; its geographical distribution and present-day prevalence are not measured.
sections.locator: Dash printed p.15; Mahanti printed p.62 / PDF p.78

sections.title: Shriya and the king: a partially recovered story
sections.text: The English introduction to an odia.org booklet tells of Shriya, a woman subjected to caste exclusion, whose devotion includes wine, meat and eggs. After she calls the king’s appearance inauspicious, he has her sons killed beneath a husking lever. Mangala restores them; the king learns a lesson, and the queen’s worship is rewarded with children. This is the booklet’s synopsis, not a verified event or a complete reading of its Odia verses.
sections.locator: PDF p.3 / printed p.1 English synopsis, web extraction only

sections.title: Reading power, dignity and devotion
sections.text: The synopsis can be read as a reversal of power: royal punishment fails to silence a socially excluded devotee, and the ruler’s household comes to recognise her goddess. That is an editorial interpretation. Shriya’s name alone does not establish that this is the same character or text as the Shreeya story associated with Manabasa; the narratives need comparison. Neither miracles nor a moral reversal establish a historical biography.

sections.title: Pana, ingredients and the act of offering
sections.text: In a 2023 Mint interview, Alka Jena explains pouring pana into a small well outside the home as an offering to Mother Earth, shared with other creatures. Swetak Abhisek Mohapatra names raw-mango pieces and a small variety of gram in the offering. These are named informants’ accounts; their description of required ingredients is not a rule verified across Odisha.
sections.locator: 14 April 2023, domestic religious practices paragraphs

sections.title: The story does not supply a universal menu
sections.text: Mahanti’s fruit-and-pana description and the booklet’s wine, meat and eggs occupy different kinds of evidence: a practice account and a story synopsis. They should not be harmonised into one menu or used to declare all Mangala worship vegetarian or non-vegetarian. The term pana also does not identify every offering as bela pana. A recipe needs its own locality, ingredients and preparation evidence.

sections.title: A literary trail, not an established beginning
sections.text: A 2009 essay by Satyabrata Das and Lalit Kumar Lenka cites Chaitra Mangala Osha at Madhya Parva, 885, in Sarala Mahabharata. The article is inspected, but its cited edition and the epic passage are not. This is a useful route toward historical evidence, not a verified founding date, proof of unchanged practice since the fifteenth century, or proof that the booklet synopsis occurs in that passage.
sections.locator: Printed p.58, first paragraph

sections.title: What a visitor can learn now
sections.text: The traditional month and named foods provide a reading route. No year-specific Tuesday, serving venue, public invitation or host permission is established. Chaitra Mangala is kept distinct from Pana Sankranti and from the autumn observance Nisha Mangalabara until source-specific relationships are demonstrated.

food_names: Pana — variant and recipe vary by account
questions: Which edition supplies Madhya Parva page 885, and what does the passage say?
Can the complete Odia booklet be recovered, read and compared with other katha witnesses?
Which households or localities document the raw-mango and gram preparation, quantities and handling?
How do local observers explain the miniature well, collective worship and sharing?

pages.name: Sathi Osha
pages.lead: A mother shapes small figures, prepares an offering and gathers her children: one household memory gives Sathi Osha a tangible place in family life.

sections.title: Which Sathi observance?
sections.text: Dash’s 2006 survey places Sathi Osha in Bhadraba and mentions turmeric images. It separately names sathi ghar on the sixth day after birth. Behera’s devotional essay also distinguishes birth-related worship from the annual Bhadraba observance. This page concerns the annual osha; shared deity names do not make the two occasions interchangeable.
sections.locator: Dash pp.15,17–18; Behera opening birth/annual distinction

sections.title: A daughter remembers her mother’s preparations
sections.text: Bishnupriya Mahapatra explicitly describes her own childhood household, noting that practices differ elsewhere. Her mother makes six flour-and-turmeric figures, wraps turmeric pieces with seven strands of thread, arranges seven plant branches and offers chakuli. She identifies the figures as Sathi and her sisters. The account also describes striking the figures and children seven times with the branches while praying for their strength; it is reported here as remembered ritual, not advice.
sections.locator: Household preparation paragraph beginning with the morning bath and new clothes; closing explanation of the figures

sections.title: From offering to a shared meal
sections.text: In Mahapatra’s recollection, the family eats the pitha after worship and her mother ties the thread-wrapped turmeric to their arms. Chakuli is therefore documented as both offering and shared food in this household. She does not supply batter proportions, fermentation time or a complete menu. The flour used for figures is not evidence of the pitha’s ingredients.
sections.locator: Offering sentence and paragraph beginning after completion of worship

sections.title: A wider devotional story
sections.text: Behera retells the story of Priyavrata and Malini, whose child is born dead. Shashthi restores the child after the king promises to spread her worship. This is his authored retelling of a broader Shashthi tradition, not a verified event or evidence that Mahapatra’s family recited it. The underlying Puranic edition has not been inspected.
sections.locator: Concluding narrative beginning with Priyavrata, son of Svayambhuva Manu

sections.title: Care, memory and practical knowledge
sections.text: An editorial reading of the household account follows a mother’s work through shaping, decorating, arranging, offering and sharing. Familiar kitchen materials acquire ritual roles; the closing meal gives children a part in the observance. The prayers express hopes for protection. Neither the use of turmeric nor the branch ritual establishes a medical benefit, and no food-science measurement is supplied. Exact plant identification and preparation knowledge require their own evidence.

sections.title: History still to establish
sections.text: The inspected 2006 description is a dated modern reference, not the observance’s origin. The first-person memory supplies continuity within one family without dating its beginning. No earliest Odisha manuscript, securely dated local katha or demonstrated historical transmission is established. The article’s six figures and seven strands or branches should not be reduced to a universal rule that every ritual object comes in sixes.

sections.title: Seasonal reading for visitors
sections.text: Mahapatra gives Bhadraba’s bright-fortnight sixth lunar day as the traditional rule. It is retained separately from any year-specific date. The documented chakuli association offers a way to learn about the season, but no serving venue, invitation or access to private worship has been verified.
sections.locator: Opening calendar paragraph

questions: Where and during which years did the remembered household practice take place?
Which dated local katha witnesses distinguish the annual osha from birth rites?
What recipe and sharing arrangements did this household use for chakuli?
Which plants do the local names designate, and how do other households describe their use?

pages.name: Nisha Mangalabara Osha
pages.lead: Night worship gives this Ashwina observance its distinctive setting. Its food, stories and local forms still need to be read source by source.

sections.title: An autumn night of worship
sections.text: Mahanti describes married women observing the osha at night in Ashwina: some on every Tuesday, others on the last Tuesday. He explains the name through its night-time observance. These are recorded alternatives, not one fixed statewide rule.
sections.locator: Printed p.58 / PDF p.74, Nisa Mangalbara osha paragraph

sections.title: Whom do the sources name?
sections.text: Dash’s April 2006 survey names Mangala. Mahanti’s description instead names Durga and mentions drawing her image with rice powder. Both labels are retained with their sources; the passages do not establish whether they describe the same local form or explain the difference.
sections.locator: Dash printed p.15; Mahanti printed p.58 / PDF p.74

sections.title: What can we say about the food?
sections.text: Mahanti records a cooked offering without naming a dish. He also reports a cock sacrifice, but does not say how the bird was used afterward. Rice powder belongs to the image-making passage. None of this supplies a recipe or a serving menu.
sections.locator: Printed p.58 / PDF p.74, image, offering and sacrifice sentences

sections.title: Significance without a claim of ritual effect
sections.text: Mahanti presents the worship as an appeal for protection from calamities. An editorial reading places women’s preparation and hopes for household security at the centre. The source does not measure whether the ritual changes outcomes, and its brief account cannot establish present-day prevalence.
sections.locator: Printed p.58 / PDF p.74, closing invocation

sections.title: A book identity, not yet a recovered story
sections.text: WorldCat records Brhat Khulana sundari, ba, Nisa Mangalabara osha, OCLC 22766659, an Odia book from Dharmagrantha Shtora in Kataka. Its date is displayed as [197-], and the cover title is Khulana sundari. This is a useful textual lead. The contents have not been inspected: the catalogue does not establish a plot, food passage, author or origin date.
sections.locator: Title, edition-date, publisher, physical-description and cover-title fields

sections.title: A modern link with maritime remembrance
sections.text: Kalinga History describes a two-day gathering at Sambhav Farm in Nayagarh, invited by Sabarmatee, with maritime discussions and a midnight visit to a temple holding Nisha Mangalabara worship. The entry was added on 24 October 2025; that is not a confirmed event date. Its framing connects the observance with concern for merchants at sea. This documents modern heritage interpretation, not the historical founding of the osha.
sections.locator: Named Nisha Mangalabara entry, date and event-description paragraphs

sections.title: History and practical knowledge still to recover
sections.text: The book identity and short modern descriptions give research a firmer starting point, but a historical narrative needs inspected editions, dated local testimony and comparison of variants. Cooking, drawing and arranging an offering involve skills; the present passages do not document their techniques or scientific explanations. A generic account of fasting or vegetarian food should not replace this observance’s specific evidence.

sections.title: How this belongs in a seasonal guide
sections.text: Ashwina is a useful cultural browsing label, with the Tuesday variants visible. No named food, current serving venue, annual date or invitation to private worship is verified. Food served at a modern heritage gathering cannot automatically become the ritual’s prescribed offering.

questions: Can OCLC 22766659 be inspected, including its title page, edition statement and food passages?
How do practitioners explain the Mangala and Durga names in particular places?
Which cooked dishes are offered and shared, and how do local preparations differ?
What dated evidence supports the maritime association beyond modern heritage interpretation?

pages.name: Pua Jiuntia
pages.lead: A mother’s vow, a thread and a shared meal provide an entry into this western Odisha observance.

sections.title: A different vow from Bhai Jiuntia
sections.text: Mahanti places mothers’ worship of Dutibahana on Ashwina’s dark-fortnight eighth day. Bhai Jiuntia follows on the bright-fortnight eighth, with sisters praying to Durga for brothers. Similar names do not make the observances interchangeable.
sections.locator: Printed p.49 / PDF65

sections.title: Offerings and the following meal
sections.text: Mahanti names puffed-rice jugara and moong-dal tikhiri as offerings. His following-day account adds a twenty-one-vegetable curry, suji manda and kheeri, shared with relatives and friends. This records a sequence, not a verified standardized recipe.
sections.locator: Printed p.50 / PDF66

sections.title: A dated Barpali account
sections.text: E Kiran Mohan’s 2011 account describes mothers assembling with plates of thread, grass, juggar and twenty vegetables. Its opening caption identifies a gathering at Tehsil Chowk, Barpali, on 1 October 2010. This is a dated local witness; it does not date the beginning of the custom.
sections.locator: Published13August2011; opening caption and ritual-plate paragraph

sections.title: Keep the differences visible
sections.text: Mohan describes Rengal-pattar wrapping and an eight-knotted thread worn at the child’s neck. Mahanti describes sal-leaf wrapping and wrist tying. The accounts also differ between twenty and twenty-one vegetables. Geography, household custom or description may explain these differences, but the evidence does not settle which.
sections.locator: Mohan following-day paragraph and plate paragraph; Mahanti pp.49–50 / PDF65–66

sections.title: Significance and the history still missing
sections.text: An editorial reading sees preparation, care and sharing made visible through household work. A fuller history still requires dated ritual texts and accounts from particular communities. We have not recovered a complete Pua Jiuntia katha in this batch. The relationship with Dutiya deserves comparison without erasing either regional identity.

sections.title: Food knowledge to investigate
sections.text: The named preparations raise useful questions about grain processing, pulse preparation, wrapping leaves and changing seasonal vegetables. Names alone cannot establish quantities, temperatures, nutritional effects or when a technique began. Record those details with a named source before writing a recipe or scientific explanation.

sections.title: Seasonal reading for visitors
sections.text: Ashwina and the lunar rule support cultural browsing. No annual date, public host, serving venue or access permission is verified. A household offering is not automatically a food visitors can buy.

questions: Which dated local katha witnesses can be inspected?
How do communities explain the vegetable, wrapping-leaf and thread variants?
Which preparation details and consensual public food offers can be independently documented?

pages.name: Bhai Jiuntia
pages.lead: Food and a returning sister’s place in the family are central questions for reading this western Odisha vow.

sections.title: Sisters, brothers and the autumn calendar
sections.text: Mahanti describes sisters invoking Durga on Ashwina’s bright-fortnight eighth day, returning to parental homes and exchanging gifts. He names jugara and tikhiri as offerings shared by sisters and brothers.
sections.locator: Printed pp.49–51 / PDF65–67

sections.title: A recent ethnographic window
sections.text: Indhubala Kesavan reports eleven months of fieldwork during May2022–December2023 in Bargarh district. The village name is a pseudonym. Her account connects married sisters’ homecoming, gifts and ritual duties with rice cultivation.
sections.locator: Printed pp.15,31–35 / PDF1,17–21

sections.title: From paddy to lia jugar
sections.text: Kesavan describes an older woman collecting household paddy, roasting and redistributing it. Stored parched rice is mixed with melted jaggery into conical lia jugar for worship, then shared. This documents collective processing and skilled labour; temperatures and proportions are not supplied.
sections.locator: Printed p.33 / PDF19; preparation and distribution paragraphs

sections.title: Honour alongside unequal treatment
sections.text: The study also records caste-separated worship and discusses women’s ritual importance alongside structural inequality. These findings belong to the study’s setting, not a statewide measurement. Food sharing does not by itself establish social inclusion.
sections.locator: Printed pp.19,33,35 / PDF5,19,21; abstract p.15

sections.title: What kind of history is this?
sections.text: The study explains contemporary practice; it does not establish an ancient founding date. We have not recovered a complete Bhai Jiuntia katha. Its rice-centred account should guide further questions about local histories, preparation and exchange rather than stand in for missing texts.

sections.title: Related traditions without collapsing identities
sections.text: Thread tying provides a useful comparison with other observances, but it cannot establish one origin or a single statewide ritual. Pua Jiuntia remains a separate profile. Dalkhai offers another contextual reading route; an association with this occasion is not proof of a scheduled performance.

sections.title: Seasonal reading for visitors
sections.text: The lunar date is a cultural label, not a confirmed event listing. Serving availability and public access remain unknown. The ethnographer’s anonymized village must not be converted into a destination or host recommendation.

questions: Can the indexed Susil Kumar Panigrahi article be recovered with its issue and pages?
Which local kathas and dated historical witnesses explain the vow?
How do food preparation and invitation customs vary across western Odisha communities?

pages.name: Nuakhai
pages.lead: The first taste of new rice opens a celebration of food, household work and renewed relationships. Nuakhai belongs here as an agrarian parba, alongside the collection’s osha and brata.

sections.title: The first rice and its season
sections.text: Mahanti describes Nuakhai, also called Nabanna, on Bhadraba’s bright-fortnight fifth day. The name joins newness with eating. His account centres the newly harvested crop; this is not evidence that every field’s harvest is complete.
sections.locator: Printed p.121 / PDF137

sections.title: What the historical account can establish
sections.text: P. K. Singh’s September2012 essay says the exact origin is unknown. It presents Ramai Dev’s adoption of the festival as oral tradition, and reports a 1991 order for a common observance day. Neither a contemporary medieval witness nor that order has been inspected here. These are research leads, not a settled founding date.
sections.locator: Printed pp.23–24 / PDF1–2; origin and calendar paragraphs

sections.title: A family’s first offering
sections.text: In Kesavan’s Bargarh fieldwork, the village priest distributes new grain. Ground new-season grain mixed with jaggery is offered to deities and ancestors, then shared with family members from a leaf bowl. This is one ethnographic account; its anonymized village is not a visitor location.
sections.locator: Printed pp.28–29 / PDF14–15; saved original visually inspected

sections.title: The meal has several documented forms
sections.text: Mahanti names jau or kheeri and arisa made with the new grain. Singh names manda pitha and khiri among offerings, then lists rice, dal, vegetables, hendua karadi khata and saga bhaja in the communal meal. These descriptions should not be merged into a compulsory menu.
sections.locator: Mahanti p.122 / PDF138; Singh p.25 / PDF3

sections.title: Skills and preparation
sections.text: Singh describes rice grinding with pestles, collecting leaves and women’s advance preparation. These details identify practical work. They do not establish measured temperatures, ratios, storage life or health benefits. Preparation names require further locality-specific evidence before becoming recipes.
sections.locator: Printed p.24 / PDF2, household preparations

sections.title: Greetings, kinship and their limits
sections.text: Kesavan describes unmarried sisters performing rites for brothers and receiving gifts, followed by greetings among neighbours. She interprets new rice and family relationships together. Her analysis also retains unequal gender roles; ritual honour cannot be treated as proof of equality.
sections.locator: Printed pp.28–31 / PDF14–17; broader gender discussion pp.27–28

sections.title: An origin comparison is not a chronology
sections.text: Mahanti suggests a connection with Vedic crop offerings. This comparative interpretation does not establish an unbroken lineage or the age of today’s Nuakhai. A stronger history needs dated texts, local records and careful comparison of changes. No single katha has been established as a universal foundation for this agrarian festival.
sections.locator: Printed p.121 / PDF137, proposed Vedic connection

sections.title: How visitors can use this record
sections.text: Bhadraba provides a browsing season, while individual event dates and serving offers need separate confirmation. The recorded dishes are leads for asking about local food. No restaurant, household invitation, public feast, annual date or booking is verified. A diaspora gathering or temple rite must be identified on its own terms.

questions: Can the original 1991 calendar/holiday order and its exact scope be recovered?
What dated evidence supports the Ramai Dev tradition, beyond later retellings?
How do offerings and calendars differ across western Odisha communities and temples?
Which named cooks can document grain processing and regional recipes, with consent?
